title: Replace Improvement Decisions With Hard-and-Fast Rules
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article proposes replacing repeated, willpower-dependent improvement decisions with fixed rules. Using the common example of exercise, the author illustrates how deciding daily whether to work out erodes over time, while committing to a firm rule — working out every day at a set time — removes the daily decision entirely. The piece extends this logic to team and organizational improvement, offering a list of sample rules leaders might adopt, from always starting meetings with a teaching moment to banning weekend email requests. The core argument is that rules sustain improvement more reliably than repeated decisions because they shift the effort from ongoing willpower to a single upfront commitment.
points: Repeated daily decisions about self-improvement, like exercising, tend to erode over time.
Converting a decision into a fixed rule removes the need to decide again each time.
The same logic applies to team and organizational improvement efforts, not just personal habits.
The article offers a list of sample rules, from meeting rituals to communication norms.
Rules are framed as commitments rather than decisions, which sustains progress more reliably.
quotes: Good leaders never lose their focus on continually improving the ingredients that make teams and team members better.
That’s why good leaders replace decisions about improvement with hard-and-fast rules.
Consistently making this choice becomes harder each day, especially as other work and goals compete with the time required.
They are no longer in the decision business. They are in the commitment business.
Rules that replace decisions surrounding improvements are commitments to do the same thing every time.
What everyday decision about improvement should you replace with a rule?
